chapter_summary:
Building a beautiful UI is only half the battle; an app becomes truly useful when it responds to user interaction. This chapter focuses on making your UI elements interactive. We'll learn how to detect when a user taps a button, retrieve the text they've typed into an `EditText`, and then use that information to update the UI or perform an action, often providing feedback through a `TextView` or a temporary `Toast` message.

The primary way to make a `Button` (or any clickable `View`) respond to a tap is by setting an `OnClickListener`. An `OnClickListener` is an interface with a single method, `onClick()`, which gets called when the view is tapped. In Kotlin, you typically implement this using a lambda expression, which makes the code concise and readable.

Let's assume you have a `Button` with `android:id="@+id/actionButton"` and a `TextView` with `android:id="@+id/resultTextView"` in your `activity_main.xml`. Here's how you'd make the button update the `TextView` when tapped:

```kotlin
import android.os.Bundle
import android.widget.Button
import android.widget.TextView
import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        val actionButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.actionButton)
        val resultTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.resultTextView)

        actionButton.setOnClickListener {
            // This code block executes when the button is tapped
            resultTextView.text = "Button was clicked!"
        }
    }
}
```
In this code, `actionButton.setOnClickListener { ... }` registers a listener. The code inside the curly braces `{ ... }` is executed whenever the `actionButton` is tapped. Here, we simply update the `resultTextView`'s text. This pattern of `findViewById` followed by `setOnClickListener` is fundamental for handling interactions.

Now, let's incorporate `EditText` to get user input. Imagine you want the user to enter their name, and when a button is clicked, a personalized greeting appears.

```kotlin
import android.os.Bundle
import android.widget.Button
import android.widget.EditText
import android.widget.TextView
import android.widget.Toast // Import Toast
import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)

        val nameEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.nameEditText)
        val greetButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.greetButton)
        val greetingTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.greetingTextView)

        greetButton.setOnClickListener {
            val name = nameEditText.text.toString() // Get text from EditText

            if (name.isNotBlank()) { // Check if input is not empty or just whitespace
                greetingTextView.text = "Hello, $name!"
                Toast.makeText(this, "Welcome, $name!", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
            } else {
                greetingTextView.text = "Please enter your name."
                Toast.makeText(this, "Name cannot be empty!", Toast.LENGTH_LONG).show()
            }
        }
    }
}
```
In this expanded example, `nameEditText.text.toString()` is how you retrieve the current text entered by the user. It's crucial to call `.toString()` because `nameEditText.text` returns an `Editable` object, not directly a `String`.

We also introduced `Toast` messages. A `Toast` is a small pop-up message that appears temporarily at the bottom of the screen and then fades away. It's excellent for providing quick, non-intrusive feedback to the user without interrupting their workflow. To create a `Toast`, you use `Toast.makeText(context, message, duration).show()`. The `context` is typically your `Activity` instance (`this`), the `message` is the text to display, and `duration` can be `Toast.LENGTH_SHORT` or `Toast.LENGTH_LONG`.

Notice the `if (name.isNotBlank())` block. This is a simple form of **input validation**. It checks if the `name` string is not empty and doesn't just contain whitespace. Input validation is a critical safety and usability measure. Without it, your app might crash if you try to perform operations on empty or invalid data (e.g., trying to convert an empty string to an integer). Always anticipate what users might enter (or not enter) and handle those cases gracefully. For instance, if you're expecting a number, you'd use `name.toIntOrNull()` to safely attempt conversion, handling the `null` case if the input isn't a valid number.

A common beginner mistake is forgetting to call `setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)` in `onCreate`. If you omit this line, your `Activity` won't know which layout file to display, and `findViewById` calls will likely result in `NullPointerException`s because the views haven't been inflated yet. Another mistake is trying to modify UI elements before they've been found via `findViewById`. Always ensure your `findViewById` calls are within or after `setContentView`.

By combining `OnClickListener`s, `EditText` input, `TextView` output, and `Toast` feedback with basic conditional logic, you can create surprisingly functional and interactive applications. This forms the backbone of almost all user interaction in Android apps.

screens.title: Handling User Input and Events
screens.subtitle: Make your app respond: buttons, text input, validation, and feedback

narration.text: In this lesson we make interfaces come alive by responding to what the user does. You will learn the core steps that let a button react to a tap, read what someone types into an EditText, and then show that result in a TextView or a short Toast message. The techniques you learn here are the backbone of interactive apps: registering a listener, converting EditText content to a usable String or number, validating that input, and providing feedback without blocking the app. For example, when a user types a name and taps Greet, you will grab the text, check that it is not blank, update a TextView with a welcome message, and show a short Toast that confirms the action. We also look at safety: why to call toDoubleOrNull or toIntOrNull before converting, and how forgetting setContentView or findViewById ordering can lead to NullPointerExceptions. By the end of the chapter you will be able to wire XML views to Kotlin, handle taps with concise lambdas, validate text and numbers, and implement a small tip calculator that demonstrates the whole flow. Ready to connect UI and code and see your app react in real time?

keyIdea.title: Interactive UI basics
keyIdea.text: Register listeners, read EditText values, validate input, update TextView and show Toasts to provide immediate, safe feedback.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Handling User Input
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Handling User Input and Events

Learn how listeners, EditText, TextView and Toasts work together to turn UI into useful behavior. We'll build a tip calculator as a hands-on example.

In this lesson
Detect taps
Use OnClickListener or a Kotlin lambda to run code when a View is tapped.
Read input
Call EditText.text.toString() and parse safely with toDoubleOrNull or toIntOrNull.
Give feedback
Update TextView and show a Toast for temporary confirmation.
Preview code
actionButton.setOnClickListener {
  val name = nameEditText.text.toString()
  if (name.isNotBlank()) {
    greetingTextView.text = "Hello, $name!"
    Toast.makeText(this, "Welcome, $name!", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
  }
}
Why this matters
Interactivity turns static layouts into useful apps. Proper validation keeps those apps reliable and safe.
Coming up
  • OnClickListener and Kotlin lambdas
  • EditText.text and safe parsing
  • Tip calculator hands-on
Explore Key Topics
Tap into the three essential areas: detect, read, and respond. Each one is small but necessary for interactive behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement listeners for user taps, retrieve typed text safely, update the UI with immediate feedback, and validate input before using it. First, you will set an OnClickListener or use a Kotlin lambda so a button executes code when tapped. Second, you will read EditText. text and convert it to a String with toString, then safely parse numbers with toDoubleOrNull or toIntOrNull. Third, you will display results with TextView and provide quick confirmations with Toast. makeText. Finally, you will apply simple conditional logic using if and else to branch on valid or invalid input and avoid crashes. Each objective includes a practical check: wiring an XML view to Kotlin with findViewById, responding to a button tap, formatting numeric output with two decimals, and showing an appropriate Toast on both success and error. These skills matter because they let you make small, robust interactive features that users expect: a greeting, a calculated tip, or a confirmation message. As you practice, watch for common pitfalls like missing setContentView or using toInt without a null-safe conversion.

screens.title: OnClickListener and Kotlin lambdas
screens.subtitle: Detecting taps and running code in response

narration.text: An OnClickListener is the mechanism Android uses to notify your code when a View is tapped. Technically it is an interface with a single callback method named onClick, and in Kotlin you can provide that behavior concisely with a lambda expression. For example, calling button. setOnClickListener { /* code */ } registers a block that executes when the button is tapped. Practically, this means you choose the reaction: update a TextView, start an Activity, or compute a value. A concrete example: when a user taps a Greet button, your lambda reads the name from an EditText and sets a greeting on the TextView. A common misconception is that listeners are complicated objects — in Kotlin they are typically tiny, inline lambdas that keep event handling readable. Remember also to avoid heavy work on the main thread inside the listener; for quick UI updates it's fine, but long-running tasks should be offloaded. To check your understanding, try replacing a verbose OnClickListener implementation with a lambda and confirm behavior is identical. The core insight is that an OnClickListener connects a user action to imperative code and with Kotlin lambdas it becomes concise, readable, and easy to test.

keyIdea.title: OnClickListener = callback for taps
keyIdea.text: Use setOnClickListener with a Kotlin lambda to react immediately when a View is tapped.

content.html:
Core Concept › OnClickListener & Lambdas
OnClickListener in Kotlin
Provide a small block of code that runs when the user taps a View. Lambdas keep this concise and readable.
val actionButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.actionButton)
actionButton.setOnClickListener {
  // runs on tap
  resultTextView.text = "Button was clicked!"
}
Example
Tap Greet, read EditText, and set greetingTextView.text to "Hello, name!".
Misconception
Listeners are heavy objects — in Kotlin they are usually simple lambdas, not bulky classes.
How it works
  • setOnClickListener registers a callback executed on tap.
  • Kotlin lambda replaces a one-method interface neatly.
  • Use for quick UI changes; avoid long blocking work there.
Key Takeaway

Use setOnClickListener with a lambda for clear, concise tap handling and keep heavy work off the main thread.

screens.title: findViewById and setContentView
screens.subtitle: Wire XML views to Kotlin safely

narration.text: Before you can respond to user actions you must connect layout views defined in XML to Kotlin variables. The essential lines are setContentView(R. layout. activity_main) inside onCreate, followed by findViewById for each view you need. setContentView inflates the layout; without it, findViewById will return null and you risk a NullPointerException. A practical example from the chapter shows binding a Button and a TextView. After setContentView, call val actionButton: Button = findViewById(R. id. actionButton) and val resultTextView: TextView = findViewById(R. id. resultTextView). A common mistake is placing findViewById before setContentView or mistyping the view ID. Another useful pattern is to keep findViewById calls compact and perform them in onCreate so your event handlers can use the references directly. If you later refactor to view binding or synthetic properties those replace findViewById, but the underlying rule remains: the layout must be inflated before obtaining view references. Practice by intentionally swapping the order to see the NullPointerException, then fix it to reinforce the correct sequence. findViewById and setContentView means always call setcontentview before findviewbyid to avoid null references and ensure views exist.. In practical terms, wire xml views to kotlin safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inflate then bind
keyIdea.text: Always call setContentView before findViewById to avoid null references and ensure views exist.

content.html:
Definition › findViewById & setContentView
Inflate layout, then get views
setContentView inflates the XML. After inflation, findViewById returns real view objects.
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
  super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
  setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) // inflate layout

  val actionButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.actionButton)
  val resultTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.resultTextView)

  actionButton.setOnClickListener { resultTextView.text = "Clicked" }
}
Common mistake
Calling findViewById before setContentView leads to NullPointerException. Always inflate first.
Quick checklist
  • Call setContentView in onCreate.
  • Then call findViewById for each view you will use.
  • Keep references local to Activity or cache them for reuse.
Key Takeaway

Inflate first, bind next. The correct order prevents null references and enables interaction.

narration.text: EditText exposes its content through a property named text, but that value is an Editable object, not a plain String. To use the typed content as a String you must call. toString() on it. For example val name = nameEditText. text. toString() produces a conventional String you can inspect, format, or parse. A concrete example is building a greeting: read the name, check name. isNotBlank(), and then set greetingTextView. text = "Hello, $name!". One subtlety is that EditText. text can be empty or contain only whitespace; isNotBlank specifically checks for non-whitespace characters and is therefore a simple, effective validation step. Another common beginner error is assuming text returns a String and attempting direct string operations without calling toString, which leads to confusing types. When expecting numeric input, call toString() first and then toDoubleOrNull or toIntOrNull on the String. Always handle the null case: toDoubleOrNull will return null for invalid input and you should treat that case with an if/else or similar guard. Practice by printing the raw Editable to the console to observe the difference, then convert it to a String and use it safely.

keyIdea.title: Call toString()
keyIdea.text: EditText.text returns an Editable. Use .toString() before parsing or comparing to avoid type surprises.

content.html:
Definition › EditText.text & toString()
From Editable to String
EditText.text is Editable. Convert to a String with .toString() before use or parsing.
val name = nameEditText.text.toString()
if (name.isNotBlank()) {
  greetingTextView.text = "Hello, $name!"
} else {
  greetingTextView.text = "Please enter your name."
}
Practical notes
  • Use isNotBlank to reject empty or whitespace-only input.
  • Call toString before parsing numeric conversions.
  • Editable implements CharSequence; treat it as transient input rather than final data.
Example

Read nameEditText.text.toString(), check isNotBlank(), then update greetingTextView and show a Toast for quick feedback.

narration.text: Toasts are a simple UI primitive for brief, non-intrusive feedback. They appear at the bottom of the screen and dismiss themselves after a short duration. Use Toast. makeText(context, message, Toast. LENGTH_SHORT or Toast. LENGTH_LONG). show() to display a message. Toasts are ideal when you want to confirm a quick action like "Tip calculated" or "Settings saved" without forcing the user to interact. An example: after computing a tip, call Toast. makeText(this, "Tip calculated!", Toast. LENGTH_SHORT). show(). A common confusion is choosing between Toast and AlertDialog: an AlertDialog requires user dismissal and interrupts flow, whereas Toasts are passive. Another note is that Toasts are not ideal for critical errors that need acknowledgement. For those, consider a visible TextView message or dialog. Also remember the context parameter: pass the Activity instance (this) so the Toast appears onscreen. When designing, use Toasts to confirm success or small errors, and keep persistent error details in the activity UI so users can fix input mistakes. Ending question: what feedback would you show via a Toast versus a persistent TextView? Toasts and user feedback means call toast.maketext with activity context to show short confirmations that do not interrupt the user.. In practical terms, provide quick, transient confirmations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use Toasts for short feedback
keyIdea.text: Call Toast.makeText with Activity context to show short confirmations that do not interrupt the user.

content.html:
Definition › Toast messages
Quick confirmations with Toast
Non-intrusive messages that automatically disappear. Good for success or short hints.
Toast.makeText(this, "Tip calculated!", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
When to use
Brief confirmations or small errors that don't require user action.
When not to use
For critical errors that need acknowledgement or detailed instructions, prefer visible UI elements or dialogs.
Design tip
Combine a Toast for quick feedback with an updated TextView that shows persistent results. Users get confirmation and a visible record of the result.
Key Takeaway

Use Toasts for short, transient messages and keep important output visible in a TextView.

screens.title: Input validation and conditional logic
screens.subtitle: Check input, convert safely, branch with if/else

narration.text: Input validation prevents crashes and improves user experience. A common flow is: read the EditText. string, validate it with isNotBlank or pattern checks, attempt a null-safe conversion like toDoubleOrNull, then use if/else to branch on the result. For numeric input, call val amount = billAmountEditText. text. toString(). toDoubleOrNull() and then check if amount!= null and amount > 0. If valid, compute tip and update the UI. If invalid, show a Toast and reset the result TextViews. This prevents NumberFormatException and handles empty or malformed input gracefully. A misconception is believing input validation only stops crashes; it also improves clarity by guiding users to correct entries and avoids unexpected results. A small example: if amount is null, call Toast. makeText(this, "Please enter a valid bill amount.", Toast. LENGTH_LONG). show() and set tip and total TextViews back to default. Practice reading the input, checking for null, and writing both success and failure branches. That habit becomes essential for any feature that consumes user-entered data. Input validation and conditional logic means read the string, parse with todoubleornull/tointornull, and use if/else to handle valid versus invalid input.. In practical terms, check input, convert safely, branch with if/else. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Validate then use
keyIdea.text: Read the string, parse with toDoubleOrNull/toIntOrNull, and use if/else to handle valid versus invalid input.

content.html:
Process Flow › Validate and Branch
Validation steps
  1. Read string: val s = editText.text.toString()
  2. Quick check: if (s.isNotBlank())
  3. Safe parse: val n = s.toDoubleOrNull()
  4. Branch: if (n != null && n > 0) { /* success */ } else { /* error */ }
Example snippet
val billAmount = billAmountEditText.text.toString().toDoubleOrNull()
if (billAmount != null && billAmount > 0) {
  val tip = billAmount * 0.15
  // update UI
} else {
  Toast.makeText(this, "Please enter a valid bill amount.", Toast.LENGTH_LONG).show()
}
Why it matters

Validation avoids crashes, leads to predictable behavior, and helps users fix mistakes. It separates parsing logic from UI updates.

Key Takeaway

Always validate and use null-safe parsing. Treat invalid input as a normal branch, not an exception.

screens.title: Tip Calculator — XML layout guidance
screens.subtitle: Design the views you'll wire to Kotlin

narration.text: The tip calculator lab starts with a simple layout. Use a vertical LinearLayout and include a TextView title, an EditText for the bill amount with inputType set to numberDecimal, a Button to trigger calculation, and two TextViews to show tip and total. Give each view an id: billAmountEditText, calculateButton, tipResultTextView, and totalResultTextView. The initial tip and total should read "Tip: $0.00" and "Total: $0.00" so users see the expected format. This layout keeps the UI clear and makes the wiring straightforward: in onCreate you will find each view by its id. A common design consideration is spacing and readability: add padding and margins so the EditText and results are easy to interact with. The chapter provides a starter XML structure; practice by adding hints and setting inputType to numberDecimal to bring up the proper keyboard. The core idea is to create minimal, semantic views that map directly to the Kotlin variables you will use in the calculation step. Tip Calculator — XML layout guidance means create a clean xml with an edittext for amount, a button to calculate, and textviews for tip and total with clear ids.. In practical terms, design the views you'll wire to kotlin. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create a clean XML with an EditText for amount, a Button to calculate, and TextViews for tip and total with clear ids.

Key Takeaway

Build a minimal layout with well-named ids so wiring and testing are straightforward.

screens.title: Tip Calculator — Kotlin logic
screens.subtitle: Find views, parse safely, compute tip and update UI

narration.text: This screen walks through the Kotlin logic for the tip calculator. In onCreate, call setContentView and then findViewById for billAmountEditText, calculateButton, tipResultTextView, and totalResultTextView. Inside calculateButton. setOnClickListener read the text with val billAmountString = billAmountEditText. text. toString() and parse it using val billAmount = billAmountString. toDoubleOrNull(). Then use an if statement to check billAmount!= null && billAmount > 0. On the success branch calculate val tip = billAmount * 0.15 and val total = billAmount + tip. Update tipResultTextView. text and totalResultTextView. text using String. format("%.2f", value) for two decimals and call Toast. makeText(this, "Tip calculated!", Toast. LENGTH_SHORT). show(). On the failure branch show a long Toast asking for valid input and reset the TextViews to Tip: $0.00 and Total: $0.00. A common mistake is calling toDouble() instead of toDoubleOrNull, which throws an exception on bad input. Practice implementing the TODOs incrementally and observing how each guard prevents a crash while producing predictable output for the user. Tip Calculator — Kotlin logic means use todoubleornull then if/else; update textviews and show toasts for success or error states.. In practical terms, find views, parse safely, compute tip and update ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Safe calculation flow
keyIdea.text: Use toDoubleOrNull then if/else; update TextViews and show Toasts for success or error states.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Tip Calculator Logic
Starter Kotlin template
val billAmountEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.billAmountEditText)
val calculateButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.calculateButton)
val tipResultTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.tipResultTextView)
val totalResultTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.totalResultTextView)

calculateButton.setOnClickListener {
  val billAmountString = billAmountEditText.text.toString()
  val billAmount = billAmountString.toDoubleOrNull()

  if (billAmount != null && billAmount > 0) {
    val tip = billAmount * 0.15
    val total = billAmount + tip

    tipResultTextView.text = "Tip: $${String.format("%.2f", tip)}"
    totalResultTextView.text = "Total: $${String.format("%.2f", total)}"

    Toast.makeText(this, "Tip calculated!", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
  } else {
    Toast.makeText(this, "Please enter a valid bill amount.", Toast.LENGTH_LONG).show()
    tipResultTextView.text = "Tip: $0.00"
    totalResultTextView.text = "Total: $0.00"
  }
}
Testing steps
  1. Enter a valid decimal like 42.50 and press Calculate.
  2. Verify tip and total update and a short Toast appears.
  3. Enter invalid input or leave blank, press Calculate, and confirm long Toast and reset values.
Key Takeaway

Implement null-safe parsing and clear success/error branches to keep your app stable and user-friendly.

narration.text: There are two approaches to converting a String to a number: the null-safe helpers toDoubleOrNull and toIntOrNull, and the direct converters toDouble and toInt. Using toDouble or toInt assumes the string is a valid numeric representation. If the user types letters or leaves the field empty, these methods throw an exception and crash the app. In contrast, toDoubleOrNull returns a null value when conversion fails, allowing you to handle the invalid case gracefully. For example, val n = s. toDoubleOrNull(); if (n!= null) { /* use n */ } else { /* show toast and reset */ }. A common beginner mistake is thinking an empty string will convert to zero; it will not — direct conversion throws a NumberFormatException. The practical rule is: always choose the null-safe helper when dealing with user input. If your domain guarantees valid input from a controlled source, direct conversion may be fine, but user-entered text is never controlled. This distinction prevents crashes and leads to simpler error-handling code paths that keep the app responsive and forgiving. toDoubleOrNull / toIntOrNull vs toDouble / toInt means todoubleornull and tointornull return null on bad input. use them with if/else to prevent numberformatexception crashes.. In practical terms, why null-safe parsing matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefer null-safe parsing
keyIdea.text: toDoubleOrNull and toIntOrNull return null on bad input. Use them with if/else to prevent NumberFormatException crashes.

Comparison › Null-safe vs direct parsing
Null-safe parsing
val n = s.toDoubleOrNull()
if (n != null) {
  // valid number
} else {
  // handle invalid input
}
Returns null on failure; lets you treat invalid input as a normal branch instead of an exception.
Direct parsing
val n = s.toDouble()
// throws NumberFormatException on invalid input
Use only when input is guaranteed valid. Not safe for user-entered text.
Key Takeaway

When reading user input, prefer toDoubleOrNull/toIntOrNull and handle the null case to avoid runtime exceptions.

narration.text: Two runtime errors you will see while learning input handling are NullPointerException and NumberFormatException. NullPointerException often appears when findViewById returns null because setContentView was not called, or the view id is wrong. The symptom is a crash when you try to use a view reference. The fix is to ensure setContentView runs before findViewById and that the id in XML matches the id used in code. NumberFormatException happens when you call toInt or toDouble on a string that is empty or contains non-numeric characters. A robust solution is to use toIntOrNull or toDoubleOrNull and then check for null. In a tip calculator, guard the conversion and display a helpful Toast when parsing fails. A good debugging technique is to log the raw string value before parsing and to reproduce input that triggers the error. Building small tests for both empty and incorrect inputs will show you how your guards work.
